evidence_quotes: Black Americans are about 13% of the U.S. population but have consistently made up roughly a quarter of people killed by police in databases like those kept by the Washington Post and Mapping Police Violence. Per capita, Black Americans are killed by police at about twice the rate of white Americans.

Comparing police killings to population share ignores differences in crime rates, police encounters, and where officers are deployed. Black Americans are also overrepresented in violent-crime offending and victimization in official data... Other analyses, including some using violent-crime suspect data as the benchmark, find Black suspects are shot at higher rates than would be expected, though the size of the gap shrinks substantially under better benchmarks.

Comparing police killings to population share ignores differences in crime rates, police encounters, and where officers are deployed... Work by Knox, Lowe, and Mummolo argues that administrative police data are themselves shaped by biased selection, so they can't cleanly identify bias in either direction... Bias can also operate upstream, through where police patrol and whom they stop.

Roland Fryer's 2016 analysis of NYPD and other data found racial gaps in lower-level force, such as handcuffing and being pushed, but no significant racial gap in officer-involved shootings once he conditioned on an encounter. His approach has been criticized, and critics argue encounter data are themselves biased.
